item.description: Stunt king Knievel treated 'positive thinking' as his method: before the jump, he didn't practice, didn't calculate angles, didn't assess risk. Psychologist Oettingen's experiments show that optimistic fantasies don't boost success—they paralyze. The Snake River failure was sealed before ignition.
item.content:encoded:
Stunt king Knievel treated 'positive thinking' as his method: before the jump, he didn't practice, didn't calculate angles, didn't assess risk. Psychologist Oettingen's experiments show that optimistic fantasies don't boost success—they paralyze. The Snake River failure was sealed before ignition.

This isn't another hero narrative; it's an anatomy of 'manifesting' put to the test: how positive affirmations led him to avoid preparation, how psychology explains it, and how engineering turned it into an accident step by step. The middle section on Napoleon Hill's life is a bit long; you can fast-forward.

2:19 When the countdown began, even he didn't believe it
On September 8, 1974, before live cameras, Evil Knievel told reporters he wished he weren't there and didn't have to do it. His usual style was to rely on positive visualization and full throttle—no calculating ramp angles, no practice, no rehearsal. But the Snake River Canyon was about 4,000 feet wide, and his previous motorcycle jump record was only 140 feet. As the countdown began, his mind held only one thought: pressing the button might be the last thing he ever did.

6:28 The stunt king's creed was taught by an insurance man
In his youth, he sold insurance to make a living, once claiming he sold 110 policies in a day, including to staff and patients at a mental hospital. He thought he deserved a vice presidency; when his boss, W. Clement Stone, refused on the spot, he quit. Stone was the co-author of Napoleon Hill's 'positive mental attitude' doctrine. Later, Knievel lived on that stuff—his future 'never prepare, just believe' approach to jumps had its roots in that insurance encounter.

10:36 The self-help pioneer's résumé doesn't survive scrutiny
Napoleon Hill is hailed as the father of modern self-publishing, author of Think and Grow Rich, interviewer of Ford and Rockefeller. But the show presents evidence that he was a fraud: no records of him advising Wilson; no archival trace of Carnegie mentoring him for the book; his interview notes 'happened' to be lost in a fire. Think and Grow Rich was actually a 230-page rewrite of his own thousand-page The Law of Success, repackaged as '13 steps to wealth,' yet it sold 100 million copies.

15:46 His first famous jump was improvised mid-air
After leaving the insurance company, to promote Honda motorcycles, he jumped 40 feet in public without a single trial run. The landing zone was a group of mountain lions and a cage of rattlesnakes. In mid-air, he realized he lacked speed but decided on the fly to lift the front wheel—the whole move was invented as he flew. He landed on the snake cage, bike and body upright, but the snakes slithered into the audience, creating a farce. It became his first 'victory' and hooked him on jumping.

24:04 The more you fantasize success, the less you clear obstacles
NYU psychologist Gabriella Oettingen's experiments clash head-on with positive thinking: students who fantasized about good grades were more likely to fail; patients who fantasized about smooth hip-replacement recovery spent more time in bed. Her explanation: optimistic fantasies let you 'pre-spend' the feeling of achievement, so you don't actually remove real obstacles; imagining obstacles is what triggers action. The show calls it counterintuitive: thinking about bad outcomes first is what makes good outcomes happen.

31:22 Two prototypes sank; the third carried a man
The Snake River jump's engineering was barely tested: the unmanned X-1 spiraled upward and nose-dived into the Snake River; the modified X-2 prototype also lost control and joined the X-1 on the riverbed. Strapped for cash, engineers reportedly even used a dog-food can for a valve. With only weeks left on the land lease, no more Skycycles were available. So the only option was to launch Knievel in the untested X-2.

34:33 His life hung on a 45-pound grip
The X-2 was registered with Idaho authorities as an aircraft. Its main controls were two: foot pedals for the tail fins, and a handle requiring 45 pounds of pressure to hold—press it and the parachute stays closed; release it or pass out, and the chute deploys immediately. He had never flown a plane, never practiced in the cockpit, and had no G-force training—just a stars-and-stripes jumpsuit. When asked if he feared blacking out mid-flight, he said no, he'd stay conscious. The narrator's point: determination is no substitute for planning.

36:41 Snake River wasn't just one failure; it was the start of decline
After ignition, everything went wrong instantly. Knievel felt 'all vision lost,' perhaps momentarily unconscious; the parachute deployed early, the craft decelerated violently, and it scraped the cliff before plunging into the Snake River near the shore. He survived. Engineer Truax's verdict: you didn't hold the handle. Knievel blamed the parachute design; harsher fans said he deliberately deployed early out of cowardice. His public performances deteriorated afterward—drinking, beating a business partner with a bat, jail time. The Snake River jump was the beginning of his long decline.

item.title: AI Giants' Enterprise Revenue: 80% from 1% of Customers, Most Kept Alive by VC
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-04-betteroffline-ai-巨头-80-企业收入来自-1-客户-多数靠-vc-续命/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-04-betteroffline-ai-巨头-80-企业收入来自-1-客户-多数靠-vc-续命/
item.description: OpenAI and Anthropic derive 80% of enterprise revenue from 1% of customers, mostly AI companies burning VC-subsidized tokens; only tech itself pays big, and when VC dries up, trillion-dollar compute bills blow up first.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI and Anthropic derive 80% of enterprise revenue from 1% of customers, mostly AI companies burning VC-subsidized tokens; only tech itself pays big, and when VC dries up, trillion-dollar compute bills blow up first.

This monologue turns the AI bubble debate from stance into structure: who the customers are at each layer, where the money comes from, and whose cash flow can break. Ten minutes pack a complete transmission chain with no fluff.

1:03 80% of enterprise revenue rests on 1% of customers
Ramp's corporate spending data shows that about 80% of OpenAI's and Anthropic's enterprise customer revenue comes from the top 1% of customers, and this ratio has not improved in the past three years. Ramp's chief economist Ara Karazian notes that this 1% is heavily skewed toward the tech industry and AI product/service companies, with a concentration he hasn't seen in any software category he tracks. The host adds a data boundary: it excludes players like Microsoft and large banks, but remains representative of the overall AI spending landscape. In other words, what truly props up the enterprise revenue of the two leading model makers is not a diversified mass market but a tiny group of extremely heavy spenders.

2:05 AI money-burners' money comes from VC, not revenue
This spending structure holds largely because AI startups rely on VC funding to sustain their burn. A common play is selling subscriptions but subsidizing tokens: a user paying $20 per month can burn $30, $40, or even $100 worth of tokens, with the difference covered by capital. That means the money OpenAI/Anthropic receive from such customers presupposes the latter can keep raising funds. The host admits this is his intuition: the loudest voices on AI Twitter are mostly VC-backed startups, and the tokens they burn internally for coding may far exceed what external customers pay. So-called real demand, at least a large chunk of it, is actually propped up by 'fundraising ability.'

4:08 Only tech itself is willing to pay big for AI
Spread these numbers out, and the conclusion is more awkward than most are willing to admit: AI has dominated every media outlet and every boardroom for three consecutive years, almost every company has tried it, and many have been approved for large AI budgets, but in the end, only the tech industry itself seems willing to spend big. Industries outside tech and AI hardly pay premium prices for large models, and there's no sign of reversal. Worse, this small group of top customers is itself unstable—they could easily switch to cheaper self-hosted open-source models or eventually move to on-device models. The host points out that this customer structure is the real underlying exposure for OpenAI and Anthropic.

5:09 Cloud vendors' fortunes rest on two model companies
The risk doesn't stop at the two labs themselves. OpenAI and Anthropic carry compute procurement commitments exceeding $1.1 trillion, and these are take-or-pay contracts—regardless of actual usage or earnings, the agreed amounts must be paid. Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Oracle, and CoreWeave's compute revenue is all betting that these two can pay. The host cites figures: OpenAI contributes about 70% of Microsoft's FY26 AI revenue; UBS estimates OpenAI and Anthropic will account for 48% of Google Cloud's total revenue next year, corresponding to roughly $84–100 billion; Barclays also gives 2027 forecasts of about $40 billion for AWS and at least $50 billion for Azure. Yet these two companies still lose billions annually.

6:10 Compute bills hit a reset wall in 2027
Why hasn't the bubble burst yet? Because the mortgage-like structure hasn't reached its peak repayment period. Such compute contracts typically involve a small upfront payment, data center capacity isn't online yet, and the real payment obligations start next month and increase month by month. The host cites an analogy from a Groundbreaker article: it's like the low teaser rate on a mortgage expiring—the rate is extremely low at signing, and after reset, the monthly payment skyrockets to unsustainable levels. Borrowers sign assuming housing prices will keep rising and they can refinance or sell the house, but when everyone tries to run at once, no one can. The massive compute commitments of OpenAI and Anthropic are the subprime mortgages of the AI bubble. The flashy deals give cloud vendors huge revenue backlogs, but the ability to pay depends on the belief in continuous growth and ever-arriving VC money.

8:11 NVIDIA's card sales rely on customer debt
The top of the chain is equally dangerous. Hyperscalers and neoclouds buy more GPUs because of demand from OpenAI and Anthropic; even those building data centers to sell to third parties benchmark against the revenue backlogs of companies like CoreWeave and Nebius—whose customers are mainly OpenAI, Anthropic, or the cloud giants behind them. More glaringly, NVIDIA's customers can no longer buy GPUs with operating cash flow alone; every purchase depends on debt remaining available. Broadcom's latest earnings also show Anthropic and OpenAI will become its top two customers. The host closes this layer with irony: 'Everything is normal, everything is fine, no one needs to panic.'

9:12 Bloomberg pops a new mega-deal, no one worries
The host notes that sell-side analysts and financial media will reassure you: the smartest people and most powerful companies don't burn money for no reason, AI demand is real, and skeptics are just cherry-picking data. But just as his monologue is about to end, a Bloomberg terminal pops up with news: Crusoe and Jane Street sign a cloud computing contract worth about $13 billion. The irony is that Jane Street is itself both a major customer of CoreWeave and a shareholder in CoreWeave—these roles intertwined are a sample of the concentration risk he's been talking about throughout the episode. He judges this to be a catastrophic capital misallocation and will be the biggest collective miss in news history.

item.title: AI Chip Design Is Real, but Verification Remains the Top Bottleneck
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-asianometry-ai-设计芯片是真的-验证仍是头号瓶颈/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-asianometry-ai-设计芯片是真的-验证仍是头号瓶颈/
item.description: AI can already write RTL autonomously, but the real bottleneck in the entire chip pipeline is verification: it consumes more than half of development time, and AI still can't answer 'what to test.' OpenAI's twenty-person team can shorten the front end, but the back end still has to be left to humans.
item.content:encoded:
AI can already write RTL autonomously, but the real bottleneck in the entire chip pipeline is verification: it consumes more than half of development time, and AI still can't answer 'what to test.' OpenAI's twenty-person team can shorten the front end, but the back end still has to be left to humans.

The author uses firsthand observations and the words of frontline engineers to rescue 'AI making chips' from clickbait: what is a prototype, what can go into production, and where the real barriers lie.

5:10 K3 has only a front end, no back end
The raw material for the 'AI tapeout in 48 hours' claim is a small inference accelerator called Nano KPU that Kimi unveiled: 238,000 parameters, about 1.46 million standard cells, 0.277MB SRAM, claiming to close timing at 100 MHz within 4 square millimeters and decode at 8,700 tokens/s. But the host looked closely: this RTL only went through functional verification, with no cell placement, routing, physical verification, or sign-off. The so-called 'timing closure' relies on estimates, and 100 MHz is not impressive even in an open-source 45nm library; human designers using the same library can achieve 20-450 MHz, and commercial processes can reach 1-3 GHz. K3's goal is not to make a good chip but to prove that an agent can autonomously reach functional completeness.

6:10 AI writing RTL is not news at all
Many people think AI writing chips started with K3, but as early as 2020, NYU used GPT-2 to generate beginner-level RTL, reporting 94.8% accuracy. The now-defunct eFabless ran an AI design contest, and Will Salcedo's GPT-4-generated design actually went to tapeout—one of the earliest known LLM-designed tapeouts. 'AI writing RTL' itself is not new; what has changed is that an agent can run unattended from scratch to functional completeness—autonomy has been distilled.

8:12 The future of agents lies in wrapping toolchains
When fully autonomous design is still out of reach, the real product form is to wrap LLMs around EDA toolchains: the LLM directs deterministic EDA tools via interfaces like MCP or APIs, much like Claude Code lets models call computer tools. Synopsys, Cadence, and Siemens all have long-term goals of opening up their stacks and handing data feedback and control to agents that can run for hours or overnight. Siemens demonstrated at Semicon Taiwan: an agent dropped hundreds of standard cells one by one into a simulator, measuring load, speed, and power for later design lookup. Repeating this tedious work for each process node is exactly the kind of thing you hand to AI before leaving work.

10:15 Even the best results keep a human in the loop
Former xAI engineer Christina Lee's post is the most convincing breakdown the host has seen. Her meta-harness has two layers: an inner layer lets the model call EDA tools to write RTL, synthesize, place and route, and verify; an outer layer lets the model review what went right and wrong in the previous round, propose improvements, and run again. The first phase only did a MAC multiply-accumulate array, iterating from 900 MHz to 1 GHz over multiple rounds; the second phase connected the MAC to SRAM and other modules, and complexity immediately rose. Note that humans have kept their hands on the wheel: the so-called goal strings are likely provided by the outer model as a reference, but the selection and final confirmation authority remain with humans. AI is not the boss; it is the co-pilot.

13:17 What is truly scary about Jalapeno is the 20-person team
OpenAI's Jalapeno demo made many people focus on 'RTL to tapeout in just 9 months.' The host reminds us: Synopsys has said elsewhere, in an unrelated context, that using their tools without AI also takes about 9 to 12 months; the chip is not complex, and the starting point is unclear—the architecture concept only began in October 2024. What really stands out is the team size: only 20 to 30 people stood up at the end of the talk. Moreover, this group's token consumption consistently ranks at the top of OpenAI's internal leaderboards, and the RTL was still being changed the day before the freeze. If such a small team can do this, the number of people needed for chip roles in the future could drop by an order of magnitude—perhaps that is why they do not emphasize it in the slides.

16:20 Verification is the real bottleneck in AI chip design
The whole industry talks up the front-end RTL but glosses over the back end: OpenAI's presentation slides spend a lot of time on spec and RTL, while the host guesses the back end was handled by partner Broadcom, thanked only on slide 34; Lee also handed the back end to Yosys/OpenLane. The asymmetry is mechanistic: PPA (power/performance/area) optimization is a closed loop—generate, verify, measure PPA—so AI has a clear reward signal; verification is not. Passing or failing a test does not tell AI how far it is from full coverage, and 'what to test' still depends on humans. Chip bugs cannot be changed once taped out, so seeing a defect on the first look at TSMC's silicon is the most crushing moment. This explains why verification can consume 50 to 70% of development time, and echoes Shibo Chen's remark that 'AI designs, humans verify' is the only reassuring approach.

17:22 The biggest enemy of front-end wrappers is OpenAI
Silicon Valley is spawning a wave of startups that wrap proprietary knowledge around frontier models to write RTL. The risk the host sees: Anthropic and OpenAI both own the models and are also making chips. If they decide to open up their models for chip design, the differentiation of front-end wrappers disappears. So he prefers teams that move toward the back end and verification, where end-to-end moats exist. How fast is this field moving? While he was writing, Architect Labs announced that its Redwood chip was fully produced and verified by AI, with specs written only by two architects; even TSMC's 3D IC talk used 'agentic AI.' The host worries that his judgment could be overturned by new news within a week or two.

item.title: The Microsoft CEO's Failed End-Run Around the NBA Salary Cap: A Star Got $48 Million for Doing Nothing
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-tbpn-微软前ceo绕开nba工资帽的败笔-球星白拿4800万不干活/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-tbpn-微软前ceo绕开nba工资帽的败笔-球星白拿4800万不干活/
item.description: What truly sank Steve Ballmer wasn't the $48 million routed to Kawhi, but that the money corresponded to no real deliverables—the 'paid to do nothing' clauses made the so-called endorsements collapse under investigation.
item.content:encoded:
What truly sank Steve Ballmer wasn't the $48 million routed to Kawhi, but that the money corresponded to no real deliverables—the 'paid to do nothing' clauses made the so-called endorsements collapse under investigation.

The first few minutes feel like sports gossip, but the rest is a complete financial audit model: four companies, fake positions, payments with no deliverables—how to see through a billionaire's carefully constructed web of fake contracts.

4:09 In the NBA, money can't buy everything
To understand why Ballmer went to such lengths, first accept a counterintuitive fact of sports: no matter how rich you are, you can't directly buy top players. NBA rules cap the total payroll for each team, designed to keep a semblance of competitive balance between big and small markets. Pablo calls it 'an interesting mix of socialism and capitalism,' and it usually suits owners fine, since every time they check the news they find themselves richer. The problem: Ballmer wanted a prime Kawhi; if he only used the team payroll route, he couldn't simply throw money at the player. So his only way was to bypass the cap by having outside companies funnel benefits to the player.

6:05 Not one crossing of the line, but the same mistake four times
What surprised Pablo in the investigation wasn't that Ballmer crossed the line, but that he made the same mistake four times. According to the NBA's investigation and Pablo's own reporting, besides Aspiration (a tree-planting/carbon-credit company), there were also scoreboard maker Daktronics, Locked In Insurance (which insured the Intuit Dome), and Boingo Wireless (which provided Wi-Fi for the Clippers)—all used to pay Kawhi Leonard. In each case, Kawhi neither filmed ads nor attended meetings. The result: four sets of documents, four groups of employees, four money flows. Pablo says that's the most fatal part—once the volume piles up, the 'I knew nothing' defense collapses, because all four companies were performing the same inexplicable task: paying a star who did nothing.

7:20 Even rich people make mistakes, because desperation comes from not being able to buy something
Many people's first reaction: Ballmer is such a shrewd businessman, he can't be this stupid. Pablo says that's precisely the most dangerous assumption. In his investigations of financial misconduct, he's seen too many 'extremely successful people' who, desperate for something money can't directly buy, do things they thought would never be discovered. In this case, what Ballmer couldn't buy wasn't the player himself, but the rule that wouldn't let him poach Kawhi directly from another team; the Lakers were also competing, and the Raptors might not let go. Ballmer's wealth let him win in almost every market, except against the salary cap. So he believed the multi-layered structure of four companies would be hidden enough. The problem: he trusted people he shouldn't have, and every step left a paper trail. Smart and crazy are not mutually exclusive.

9:30 Kawhi's insistence on doing nothing was the fatal flaw of the fake contracts
The truth of the entire arrangement is visible from Kawhi's own attitude. Pablo recounts that Kawhi was explicit: for this off-the-books money, he didn't intend to do anything for it—he wouldn't work for the payers, but he wanted the money. Ballmer's answer: no problem, we'll handle it. There was no business deliverable that could be defended as an 'endorsement fee'—no ads, no appearances, no social content, not even a formally announced contract. When a real audit chases the money, the first question is: what did you buy with this payment? If the answer is 'nothing,' the whole multi-layered structure collapses. Payments with no deliverables are always the most glaring item in the paper trail.

11:30 The heaviest owner fine in history, whose real purpose was to block arbitration
The NBA's punishment of Ballmer is the heaviest ever for an owner: five first-round picks, a $30 million fine, plus $50 million to cover the league's legal fees, and a one-year ban from entering the Intuit Dome—the arena he spent $2 billion building, so beloved he personally measured the bathrooms. To Ballmer, the numbers are just 'rounding errors,' but the real design is procedural: the NBA let Kawhi off with a relatively light penalty, Kawhi accepted the settlement, and the arbitration route was legally cut off. Ballmer's only remaining path to overturn it would be a civil lawsuit, which would mean more document disclosures—the last thing he wants is more details exposed to public view. On the surface it's a heavy fine, but underneath it's about sealing off the other side's only safe exit.

15:05 Five first-round picks gone, yet the team's valuation still rises
The impact on the Clippers' competitive future is indeed significant: the next first-round pick they're eligible to make, in Pablo's words, hasn't even reached puberty. But from another angle, the punishment doesn't change the team's financial value. Pablo estimates that if the Clippers were truly sold, they wouldn't fetch the Lakers' $12.5 billion, but they'd sell for more than most expect—because sports assets have decoupled from revenue: scarcity is there, and valuations operate in a different system. The host put it more bluntly: sports and private markets are 'nakedly tied together.' The lesson for founders: when an asset becomes a scarce license, no matter how ugly the fundamentals, the price can still defy common sense.

20:40 Ballmer's return to Seattle must pass the 29-owner gauntlet
What Ballmer really wants may be Seattle: to bring an NBA team back to his hometown. But that's also the most overlooked chain in this whole saga—any new team must be approved by the existing 29 owners, and those 29 owners are precisely the group that pushed the NBA to issue the heaviest fine in history. The longer Ballmer chooses to 'go to war,' the worse his standing in that club; even if he wins in court, it would be nearly impossible to buy a team again in the future. Pablo half-jokes: if you're going to buy a new team, don't make enemies of the 29 owners who need to approve you. In power structures, the most expensive thing is never the fine—it's the peer vote.

item.title: When Will the AI Bubble Burst? Watch Credit Default Swaps and Token Prices
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-excessreturns-ai泡沫何时破-紧盯信用违约互换与token价格/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-excessreturns-ai泡沫何时破-紧盯信用违约互换与token价格/
item.description: The AI bubble will eventually burst, but current valuations are far below the dot-com era, with Nvidia's P/E at just 15x. The real risk lies in the credit markets, where credit default swaps have risen to historic highs, signaling a potential sharp correction ahead.
item.content:encoded:
The AI bubble will eventually burst, but current valuations are far below the dot-com era, with Nvidia's P/E at just 15x. The real risk lies in the credit markets, where credit default swaps have risen to historic highs, signaling a potential sharp correction ahead.

Dan Niles offers quantitative indicators for judging the AI bubble (token prices, cloud margins) and unique perspectives (credit markets, Chinese semiconductors), providing practical reference for understanding the current market phase.

4:03 Token prices down 50% but usage up 2.5x
Dan Niles points out that to judge whether the AI bubble has peaked, you need to watch two core variables: token production and unit price. Since the end of May, due to competition from open-source models, token unit prices have fallen about 50%, but production has grown 2.5x over the same period. As long as production growth offsets price declines, industry revenue is still expanding. Meanwhile, revenue growth at the three major cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) accelerated from 35% in March to 43% in June, with operating margins up about 2 percentage points, indicating the industry's fundamentals remain healthy.

7:03 4x leverage was the main cause of the fund blowup
The Situational Awareness fund blowup was not due to wrong positioning but the use of 4x leverage. If the underlying dropped 25%, 4x leverage would lose 100%, triggering liquidation. This echoes the lesson of Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) in 1998. After hearing about the fund's problems on July 29, Dan Niles judged that a short-term bottom was near because fundamentals (token usage growth) had not deteriorated. He warns that leverage amplifies risk in both directions, and when long and short positions are simultaneously unfavorable, it can trigger catastrophic selling.

9:12 Cloud providers' cash flow turns negative for the first time
Despite accelerating revenue and improving margins at cloud providers, the market worries about deteriorating free cash flow. For example, Google's cash flow turned negative for the first time since going public, due to massive AI capital expenditures. Dan Niles believes this resembles the dot-com era: the technological revolution is real, but stock prices can still crash 78% (Nasdaq 2000-2002). He expects strong industry growth over the next year, but if a hyperscaler cuts capital spending due to debt problems, it could trigger a chain reaction.

14:19 Data center political risk is the biggest short-term threat
Dan Niles points out that the biggest short-term risk to AI growth is not demand but political resistance. A Gallup poll shows 71% oppose building data centers in their backyards, higher than the 53% who oppose nuclear plants. Both parties are unusually united against data centers, especially in red states like Texas. Hyperscalers have failed to effectively communicate the jobs and tax benefits data centers bring, while anti-business forces have successfully cast them in a negative light. He expects political risk to weigh on the market until the November midterm elections.

21:28 Chinese semiconductors will break the cyclicality myth
Dan Niles believes that the view that semiconductors are no longer cyclical is dangerous, and China may be the key to breaking this myth. He draws parallels to Japan in the 1980s and South Korea in the 1990s, which entered the DRAM market with government support and eventually displaced US dominance. Today, China's CXMT (长鑫存储) and YMTC (长江存储) are expanding rapidly: CXMT plans to raise monthly capacity from 300,000 wafers to 500,000, and YMTC aims to surpass Samsung and SK Hynix in NAND. For China, semiconductor self-sufficiency matters more than aircraft carriers.

27:18 Agentic AI will extend the cycle by at least a year
Dan Niles believes agentic AI is a new phase, marked by the launch of the OpenClaw project on January 30 this year. The agentic phase consumes 10-100x more tokens than conversational AI, which will sustain demand growth. He expects the stock market to have at least another year of upside, but warns of competition from Chinese memory chips. He advises investors to watch the data like a hawk and avoid excessive optimism or pessimism.

30:43 Software faces AI disruption; security and gaming relatively safe
Dan Niles believes AI's impact on the software industry is enormous. OpenAI and Anthropic's combined annualized revenue surged from $29 billion at the start of the year to $105 billion seven months later, and that spending must squeeze other software budgets. He sees three relatively safe areas: cybersecurity, recording systems, and video games. Recent deals like Salesforce partnering with Anthropic and Workday being acquired by Silver Lake suggest software stocks may be near a bottom, but security valuations are already high.

39:23 Credit markets are the early warning system for the AI bubble
Dan Niles emphasizes that credit markets are key to judging the AI bubble. He monitors daily the credit default swap (CDS) prices of hyperscalers like Microsoft, Google, and Nvidia, and finds they are higher than the North American investment-grade average and at historic highs. Credit investors are more cautious than equity investors because bond returns are fixed, so they must ensure principal safety. AI's massive capital expenditures rely on debt financing, and the 30-year Treasury yield has risen to its highest since 2007, increasing financing costs and potentially becoming the trigger for the bubble's burst.

item.content:encoded:
The tell of AI writing isn't style but the 'information padding' where output exceeds input. The hedge fund titan's public admission about his AI-written op-ed became a turning point—Pangram's fourth generation has a false positive rate of about 1 in 24,000, and the more models converge, the easier they are to catch.

The CEO himself breaks down the classifier's principles, how training data is created, the false positive rate metrics, and even debunks a common type of 'false accusation' complaint as astroturfing. For decision-makers judging the authenticity of AI writing, the information density is high.

4:00 The real question isn't 'did you use AI' but where the ideas came from
Event: Stanley Druckenmiller published an op-ed in WSJ that was obviously AI-written to a discerning eye; someone ran it through Pangram and got a 100% AI score. The turning point was that he didn't hide it—he openly admitted, 'I'm essentially not a good writer, I just used AI,' and WSJ refused to retract it. Bryan pushed further: since he admitted it, why not reveal the prompt? 'Did you use AI' is a false dichotomy; the real question is where the ideas came from—whether it's 'help me write an op-ed against the Treasury's action' or 'here are my five pages of notes, help me polish them into an essay.'

13:00 Detecting AI is theoretically impossible, but practically sufficient
In 2023, Max asked research friends whether AI text could be detected; the unanimous answer was 'impossible, don't try, and models will only get stronger.' Pangram's response was to abandon theoretical counterexamples (like 'have ChatGPT paraphrase any text to disprove it') and focus only on practical scenarios: when the input information is less than the output, that's a trace of AI involvement, which Bryan calls word inflation. This definition also explains why early Yelp/Amazon fake reviews didn't become a breakthrough—platforms felt AI reviews were only 3% and not worth the trouble.

34:30 Catching AI isn't about em dashes but synthetic mirroring
Pangram is a classifier model, not a surface-level rule detector like em dash checkers. The approach: take an open-source LLM, cut off the 'predict next token' head, and replace it with a classification head that outputs a 0-15 AI involvement score. Training data is created via 'synthetic mirroring': take human-written articles, have an LLM compress them into prompts (like 'write a 200-word piece covering these three points'), then feed those to random frontier models to get a human/AI pair on the same topic. The second layer is editing prompts, with clause-level annotation: unchanged parts are human, modified parts are AI-assisted, and entirely new sentences are AI-generated.

40:00 A detector's lifeline is false positive rate, not accuracy
Pangram 4 has a false positive rate of about 1 in 24,000, measured by running millions of pre-2022 documents (when AI ghostwriting was nearly impossible); the false negative rate is about 1 in 300, measured by regenerating with frontier models from real user prompts in WildChat. Not perfect, but the direction is right. Bryan's experience is that false positives are extremely low, and that's the lifeline for whether the product can be seriously used. Pangram 4's step change came from switching from a 512-token window to token-level output: even a fully human-written document with two AI sentences in the middle can be pinpointed word by word.

46:00 Detectors don't need to be 100% accurate, just make cheating costly
Max says education is a huge market, and this year is the first time people realize 'there actually exists a usable AI detector.' The product logic isn't 100% precision but creating friction on the shortcut—making 'throwing homework at AI' go from zero cost to having a cost, so students will take the next easiest path, which is doing it themselves. This judgment applies equally to enterprise contexts: Oxide's hiring is a writing-intensive process, and LLM-generated boilerplate in 'why I want to join Oxide' is instantly recognizable; the detector just makes it explicit.

50:00 Most 'I was falsely accused' sob stories are astroturf ads
Max distinguishes two types of opposition. One group genuinely wishes detectors didn't exist: it allows the AI text they produce professionally to be authoritatively identified. The other is the marketing of the humanizer ecosystem: these tools claim to rewrite AI text to fool Turnitin and Pangram, selling to students caught cheating; they typically also come with their own 'AI detector' that first judges your text as AI, then sells the rewriting service. Many Reddit posts complaining 'my teacher falsely flagged me 76% AI and gave me a zero' are astroturf for this lead generation—run them through Pangram and they're all AI-written.

59:00 Stronger models haven't made detection harder, but easier
Asked if they're forever chasing frontier models, Max gives a counterintuitive judgment: two things happen simultaneously—models get smarter, but post-training repeatedly teaches 'correctness' and preferences, narrowing the output distribution far more than in the GPT-2 era. GPT-2 tried to mimic the full distribution of human output; today's models only give 'correct' tokens, not what an ordinary person would say. His and Oxide's three hosts' gut feeling aligns: new models speak with a certain 'strangely erudite' flavor, and detection hasn't gotten harder—it's actually easier to get started.

1:01:00 The next battleground is how much the human actually input
Pangram can already guess the model family internally: the probe's top-1 accuracy is 90%, but productization would need to reach 98%. A further direction is 'reverse Pangram'—inferring what prompt might have generated a text and how much context the model had: two key points or fifteen? The information content of this dimension changes the characterization of Druckenmiller's op-ed completely—giving five pages of notes to polish is collaboration; giving five bullet points to expand is ghostwriting. The next battleground for detection isn't 'did you use AI' but 'how much did the human actually input.'

item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, with interceptor drones costing about $2,000 to shoot down Russian Shaheds worth over $50,000. AI guidance is already in combat, but full autonomy remains distant.

This episode offers a rare, direct account from a top Ukrainian drone maker of the real forms, costs, and AI boundaries of battlefield drones. Dense with information, it's directly valuable for understanding modern warfare and the drone industry.

4:07 Producing nearly 100,000 a month, capacity still expanding
Founded in 2023, General Cherry initially produced only about 10 drones a month; now monthly output is around 100,000 (exact number undisclosed). The company works with over 110 military brigades, with the best units consuming more than 5,000 drones a month. Capacity is still growing because battlefield consumption is enormous—drones have become expendables.

7:09 Hundreds of drone companies in Ukraine, but only 10–15 at the top
Ukraine may have up to 2,000 drone companies, but the vast majority are garage-style small workshops. Only 10 to 15 large companies can produce 1,000 to 10,000 drones a month, and General Cherry claims to be in the top five. This fragmented yet vast industrial ecosystem is the foundation of Ukraine's rapid innovation, but it also means intense competition.

8:14 AI models developed in-house, deep co-creation with the military
General Cherry's AI guidance system is fully self-developed, backed by a strong R&D department, and works closely with military units on the front lines. They gather battlefield feedback daily through mobile teams and iterate products quickly. This 'R&D–combat–feedback' loop lets Ukrainian drone technology adapt rapidly to the battlefield, rather than relying on external procurement.

10:20 Rocket-shaped FPV originated with Red Bull, not Ukraine
This rocket-shaped FPV drone is not a Ukrainian original; it was first used by Red Bull in 2021 or 2022 for sports events. Ukrainian companies discovered this shape could achieve higher speeds than standard quadcopters, so they adopted and optimized it. This reflects the fast-learning, pragmatic nature of Ukraine's drone industry—not seeking originality, only effectiveness.

17:24 A $2,000 interceptor drone against a $50,000 Shahed
General Cherry's interceptor drones (such as the Bullet) cost about $2,000 yet can shoot down Russian Shahed drones worth $50,000 to $100,000. This asymmetric cost exchange is key to Ukraine's strategy against Russia's 'saturation attacks'—using cheap drones to exhaust the enemy's expensive assets while avoiding wasting Western-supplied costly air-defense missiles.

21:28 Interceptors confirmed to have downed over 5,000 Russian drones
General Cherry's tactical interceptor drones (General Trajectory Air) have confirmed over 5,000 Russian drone kills since production began in February 2025, with over 1,000 Russian 'Moniya' drones downed in December alone. The Shahed-interceptor model entered mass production in December 2025, with confirmed kills nearing 1,000. These numbers show interceptors have become a significant force in battlefield air defense.

23:28 AI runs on-device, not in the cloud
General Cherry's AI guidance model runs on the drone's local camera chip, not in the cloud. After an operator detects a target via radar and launches the drone, the AI automatically identifies and locks onto the target without human intervention. This edge-AI design avoids battlefield communication delays and jamming, which is key to its practical viability.

27:32 Fully autonomous weapons are a terrifying future, but AI is inevitable
Marko admits that if drones become fully autonomous, it will be terrifying—killing would no longer require another human, only robots or drones. Currently they use semi-autonomous AI only on interceptor drones, because adding AI to standard FPVs would significantly raise costs, making it better to buy more non-AI drones. But he predicts AI technology will spread quickly and prices will drop, making future battlefields even more brutal.

item.title: The Wow! Signal Remains Unsettled After Nearly 50 Years: It Looked Like an Alien Call, but the Second Call Never Came
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-isaacarthur-wow信号近50年没落定-它像外星呼叫-却再没来第二声/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-isaacarthur-wow信号近50年没落定-它像外星呼叫-却再没来第二声/
item.description: That 72-second narrowband hydrogen-line signal from 1977 has never repeated, and it falls short of the bar for evidence of an alien civilization. Its legacy is not an answer but a reminder: in a noisy universe, discovery and proof are separated by an entire galaxy.
item.content:encoded:
That 72-second narrowband hydrogen-line signal from 1977 has never repeated, and it falls short of the bar for evidence of an alien civilization. Its legacy is not an answer but a reminder: in a noisy universe, discovery and proof are separated by an entire galaxy.

Those expecting a definitive conclusion will be disappointed; those wanting to understand how a single anomaly becomes—or fails to become—evidence will find a complete framework for judgment.

3:09 The 72-second length comes from Earth's rotation
Big Ear is a transit telescope—it doesn't move to track targets but relies on Earth's rotation to sweep the sky overhead. A point source fixed on the celestial sphere naturally takes about 72 seconds to cross the beam—exactly 1/1200 of a day. So the duration doesn't mean the sender deliberately spoke for only 72 seconds. What matters is the gain curve: a true source enters the beam, strengthens, exits, and weakens. The Wow! signal fits this pattern completely, and any terrestrial interference explanation must first pass this test.

5:10 6EQUJ5 is an intensity curve, not a code
6EQUJ5 is the signal strength reading under Big Ear's early print format: each symbol represents about a 12-second observation window, with digits and letters indicating multiples above background noise. In time order they are 6, 14, 26, 30, 19, 5—strong in the middle, weak at the ends, like a brightness curve written sideways. Renormalized to a 1–100 scale, they become 17, 40, 74, 86, 54, 14. The host's quip is memorable: if an alien's first message looks like an invalid software activation code, that's a reasonable opening.

7:11 It hugs the hydrogen line but misses by 50 kHz
1420 MHz is the radio spectral line of neutral hydrogen—a natural landmark of the universe's most abundant element and SETI's most commonly assumed calling frequency. Because Big Ear's master oscillator was set 0.1 MHz high, the Wow! signal's frequency, after correction, has two interpretations: 1420.356 MHz or 1420.456 MHz; the true hydrogen line is about 1420.406 MHz. Both are only about 50 kHz off—as if deliberately avoiding hydrogen noise while using the line as a coordinate. Yet this position is also full of natural hydrogen cloud sources; intelligence and coincidence cannot be distinguished by frequency alone.

11:13 One horn received it, the other didn't
Big Ear had two adjacent feed horns. A source fixed on the celestial sphere, swept by Earth's rotation, should enter both horns sequentially and be recorded twice. The Wow! signal appeared in only one horn, and the records don't say which, leaving two candidate positions in the sky. Possible explanations include: the source shone only briefly, a narrow beam just grazed us, or interference came from nearby. All subsequent searches—including Breakthrough Listen's 2022 effort using Green Bank and the Allen Array to look for Sun-like stars in the candidate regions—found no repeat. The lack of a second detection is the core reason it hasn't made the confirmed list.

15:17 Terrestrial interference and satellites are hard to mimic
Earth is noisy, but a true candidate must pass the 72-second profile test: an ordinary aircraft crossing the beam wouldn't take that long; low-Earth-orbit satellites typically sweep across in seconds. A satellite in high orbit, using side lobes, or in a special orbit would require a chain of coincidences. Ground transmissions in the 1420 MHz band are internationally protected, but illegal devices or faulty electronics could produce out-of-band signals leaking through antenna side lobes. There's also an effect called interstellar scintillation that can briefly brighten a distant signal, but that requires a source to be amplified in the first place. None of these explanations is perfect, which is why the mystery survives.

19:18 A magnetar could pump a hydrogen cloud into a maser
A natural explanation derived from Arecibo archive research: a high-energy transient—like a magnetar flare—pumps atoms in a cold neutral hydrogen cloud into population inversion, briefly turning the cloud into a natural microwave maser, much like a laser amplifying microwaves. This could explain several things at once: the signal came from space, near the hydrogen line, strong enough, yet appeared only once; the cloud was glowing when the first horn swept over it and had faded by the time the second horn arrived. The host says this is his personal favorite because it solves multiple puzzles in one mechanism, but it remains a speculative path with no hard evidence.

27:27 Becoming a discovery requires passing four gates
If such a signal is received again in the future, to be called a true technosignature it needs at least four conditions: first, repetition at the same location, showing it's still there; second, simultaneous reception by telescopes at two different sites, ruling out terrestrial interference; third, modulation, encoding, or mathematical structure rather than a pure carrier wave; fourth, systematic exclusion of known natural processes. Historically, pulsars were nicknamed 'Little Green Men' when first discovered, showing that nature can perfectly mimic intelligence. The right approach is not to take sides—believing or mocking—but to allow excitement and then do everything possible to prove you're fooling yourself.

31:29 Its legacy is a window too narrow
The Wow! signal appeared in the form early SETI hoped to see—narrowband, near the hydrogen line, strong enough, shaped like a real celestial source—for 72 seconds, and then nothing more. It shows what a great discovery looks like before it has gathered enough evidence. The host's conclusion: the galaxy is 100,000 light-years wide and billions of years old; even the grandest civilization is just a flickering spark within it. If civilizations don't spread, signals aren't frequent, and beams don't often point our way, the Fermi paradox may not exist. The Wow! signal, in that 1/1200 of a day, briefly placed that possibility before humanity.

item.title: Land is not a commodity: why a land value tax can cure the housing crisis
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-moneymacro-土地不是商品-地价税为何能根治住房危机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-moneymacro-土地不是商品-地价税为何能根治住房危机/
item.description: The housing shortage is only the surface; the real disease is land monopoly: a land value tax shifts the burden from buildings to land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, returning location value to society instead of enriching landlords.
item.content:encoded:
The housing shortage is only the surface; the real disease is land monopoly: a land value tax shifts the burden from buildings to land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, returning location value to society instead of enriching landlords.

The land value tax is an overlooked lever that economists on both left and right agree on. Lars Doucet uses cases like Houston parking lots, Korea's assessment system, and Norway's resource dividends to turn an abstract tax into a story of power struggle.

0:05 A land tax is not a property tax; it's a location tax
Lars opens with a metaphor: the land value tax shares a root with ordinary property tax but splits 'building value' from 'land value.' A building tax punishes you for building, maintaining, and renovating; a land tax only punishes you for occupying a prime location and letting it sit idle. He says land's value comes from the labor of those around you—the fact that you can step out and earn, study, and make friends depends on your neighbors and the whole city. Landlords lie back and siphon this collective value into their own pockets. That's the paradox of 'Progress and Poverty': a ballpoint pen fell from $270 to 11 cents, but land never does.

0:13 The build-more crowd is right, but not enough
The host asks: Oakland relaxed density and rents fell—do we still need a land tax? Lars admits the 'housing shortage' is the main cause, but points out that the YIMBY crowd can't explain a counterexample: Houston has no zoning, yet downtown still has a giant surface parking lot worth $500 million. Why? Because the property tax bundles land and buildings together; the more you build, the more you pay, while hoarding and waiting for appreciation is cheap. So developers have no incentive to develop, only to lobby for rezoning and then keep hoarding. He says reform without a land tax will hit the impasse of 'you changed the zoning, but I still won't sell.'

0:23 The objections are born of imagination
Lars groups the opposition into three types and dismantles each. How do you separate land from buildings in assessment? He says about 14,000 assessment jurisdictions worldwide already do something similar; South Korea manually reviews 500,000 sample parcels each year and produces a nationwide land value map in five months; Norway trains a national automated valuation model on the Finn.no property data platform, with a core team of just three people. Worried about protests? He says the real source of protest is 'my land looks the same as my neighbor's, why am I charged more'—under a land tax, your assessment basis is the same location as your neighbor's, so it's actually easier to calculate. The excuse for not implementing is that it hasn't been measured.

0:35 Little old ladies are not a reason to object
The sharpest criticism is 'transition unfairness'—the day a land tax is announced, existing landowners instantly bear the capitalization of all future tax liabilities, an expropriation in one stroke. Lars acknowledges this is a Gordon Tullock-style transition trap, then offers safeguards: action is never a one-step national 100% land tax, but a gradual switch by school district or county; run revenue-neutral simulations, and most single-family homes see their tax bill fall. As for the elderly worried about being driven out of their homes, he says Texas already has a tax deferral system: you owe it, and after death it's deducted from the estate with interest.

0:41 Britain's failure is a capacity problem
The most common counterexample online is Britain's 1910 'People's Budget': valuation took six years and was overturned by shopkeeper protests and the courts. Lars's response is blunt: the much-discussed article is 'inferring a universal law from a single sample,' and simultaneously claims 'a pure land tax has never succeeded' and 'land cannot be valued'—yet South Korea has been assessing national land values parcel by parcel for decades. He says this only proves Britain's state capacity was weak, not that the land tax is theoretically unworkable. His tone hardens: if you want to be a serious critic, go find counterexamples, don't pass off lazy ignorance as settled truth.

0:45 Norway achieves Georgism through resource dividends
Lars points to a fact that makes today's Norway a 'success story': the entire Norwegian resource management system is Georgist in structure—oil and other natural resources are deemed the property of all the people, extractors pay a very high resource tax, but production and investment themselves are not penalized, thus encouraging entrepreneurship while channeling the natural dividend into the state treasury to subsidize universal welfare. Norway's Georgism is almost perfect, except it doesn't apply to land value tax. This 'Norwegian paradox' leads him to assert: the land tax is not the enemy of the welfare state; it can be its foundation.

0:51 The car opened a second frontier
Lars explains why the land question that filled the air 100 years ago disappeared: the frontier itself was a kind of 'free land' mechanism—as long as you could expand into the wilderness, the lower classes didn't have to face the squeeze of 'high work plus high rent.' America's first frontier was westward expansion; after it closed came Henry George. In the 20th century, the car turned the suburbs into a 'second frontier,' extending the reprieve another 80 years, until it closed again around 2006–2008. He says some now call this the 'second Gilded Age,' but it's just the same script from a hundred years ago with a new cast, and post-pandemic remote work as a 'third frontier' lasted only about five minutes before capital digested it.

0:53 Don't win online; do homework for politicians
The closing answer is practical: Lars says the most effective way to create change he's learned in the past five years is not arguing with keyboard warriors, but preparing data simulations and ready answers for every objection a state senator or city councilor might raise, and putting them directly on their desks—he calls 'doing homework for politicians' an absurd but remarkably effective strategy. Today several states have passed bills allowing land value tax reform. His action advice: go measure, don't guess.

item.title: What Drives Founders Isn't Becoming a Billionaire—It's Fear of the Server Crashing at 3 AM
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-ycsp-驱动创始人的不是当亿万富翁-是怕服务器半夜崩掉/
