item.description: Most people think wealth ambition gets you through a startup. Paul Graham says what actually pushes you day to day is disaster fear—the server crashing, the model train about to fall off the table. You look up after a decade of heads-down work and realize that at the last round's valuation, you're already a billionaire.
item.content:encoded:
Most people think wealth ambition gets you through a startup. Paul Graham says what actually pushes you day to day is disaster fear—the server crashing, the model train about to fall off the table. You look up after a decade of heads-down work and realize that at the last round's valuation, you're already a billionaire.

After 21 years and 47 batches, PG's take: AI has barely changed anything about startups—only the bill. Good for calibrating your confidence in 'this time is different.'

2:02 Those nostalgic for the golden age forget it only had Reddit
People have been saying YC is past its prime since around 2008. PG's read: to attack it, you first have to admit it was once great, so you can only ever say 'it's not what it used to be.' But his counterexample is concrete: the代表作 of the so-called good era is Reddit, while this episode's office hours project is intercontinental ballistic cargo—like an ICBM, except instead of exploding on landing, it unloads. Another category is curing cancer. He says there are too many approaches—vaccines on one end, therapies on the other—so you should invest in several; any one succeeding makes it worth it. One company this episode does on-demand research for cancer patients, and what he likes is exactly that approach: cancer is famously not solved by 'thinking of one cure'; maybe the way to beat it is death by a thousand cuts.

4:09 Google won't be breached; it will be obsoleted by the world
Many ideas from the 2012 'frighteningly ambitious' essay have already been done, including 'a new Google.' PG says he predicted the path back then: you can't attack Google head-on; you wait for the world to change until its model is obsolete. OpenAI is that change itself—after using it, he no longer uses search, because what he always wanted wasn't web pages but information, so he just asks the AI. This is a corollary that holds for all incumbents: moats aren't breached; they're obsoleted.

6:15 Ambition is the entry ticket; daily fuel is fear of looking bad
Ambition is necessary because startup obstacles are too terrifying to get through on conscientiousness alone. But PG says what actually moves a founder at any given moment isn't 'solve this and I'll be a billionaire' but disaster fear: the server crashing, fear of looking like a fool. His image is a toy train—the engine is about to fall off the table edge, and you rush to catch it. You spend ten years heads-down fixing the train, look up at the last round's valuation, and find you're already a billionaire. He says sometimes he's the one who calculates it first and tells the founder.

9:21 The only test of formidable is getting what you want
Formidable is a private word PG and Jessica used even before YC. His definition is operational: this person can get what they want in any situation—if they can't, how are they formidable? This definition incidentally explains the investment logic: you hold stock in their company, they hold it too, interests are aligned; they get what they want, you get what you want. It's also the precondition for his answer to where the next trillion-dollar company comes from.

11:24 Lean startup isn't dead: even rocket companies can start small
Asked whether lean startup is dead and you now have to burn big money from day one, PG's rebuttal has two layers. First, price: tokens are expensive now only because of GPU shortage; the price for the same level of reasoning drops about 30x per year, and you're also getting higher-quality tokens—technology always gets cheaper. Second, path: even rocket companies can start with modest money. You can't build a real rocket, but you can build the design, run simulations, show experts—if convincing enough, you get the next round. StarCloud wrote a white paper and booked one launch—though he added that the founder is a known expert in the field with built-in credibility; a fresh graduate wouldn't have it so easy.

13:24 AI went the wrong way: from human toward perfect, not perfect toward human
In the 1980s, AI people thought the path was from a 'perfect fly'—doing only fly things but doing them as well as a fly—then climbing up to mouse, cat, monkey, human, each level perfect. What we got is the reverse—a full human right away, but one that spouts nonsense, like an undergrad trying to bluff through a paper. What got optimized is the opposite dimension: not from perfect toward human, but from human toward perfect. This also explains the jagged frontier: it can solve math problems but can't tell you what time a restaurant opens.

16:30 AI changes the bill structure, not shipping speed
PG says the best predictor of startup success is still shipping speed, and AI hasn't replaced that metric—with these tools in hand, plenty of companies this episode still don't ship fast enough, showing the difference isn't in how fast you can write things; you first have to come up with the ideas. 'With AI, what hasn't changed?' His answer: so far, almost everything is exactly the same. The only strange new thing is the bill structure—before, the big cost of a startup was salaries, everything else was cheap by comparison; now there's GPU, and tokens can burn tens of thousands of dollars a day.

19:36 The next trillion-dollar company comes from the right people, not the right idea
Asked where the next trillion-dollar company will come from, PG switches the question from track to people: it comes from the right founder, not a specific idea—startup ideas are highly variable, and he'll only say 'probably not dog walking.' Conversely, to judge whether a company is worth investing in, first judge whether the founder is formidable; what they're working on is likely promising. As for whether future founders will look different, he says there's already 20 years of data: today's founders are exactly the same as 20 years ago, and there's no reason they'd change in another 20.

item.title: Arm Builds CPUs: The Biggest Bottleneck in Chip Design Is Verification, Not Design
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.description: The real time sink in the chip cycle is verification, debugging, and documentation, not RTL; Arm already has 80%-90% of engineers using AI daily and has broken its 98.5% gross margin licensing model to build CPUs itself.
item.content:encoded:
The real time sink in the chip cycle is verification, debugging, and documentation, not RTL; Arm already has 80%-90% of engineers using AI daily and has broken its 98.5% gross margin licensing model to build CPUs itself.

Get Arm's internal real data on AI's usefulness in chip design, then see product, capital, and supply chain judgments form a closed loop—worth benchmarking for AI infrastructure practitioners.

3:43 Arm builds CPUs itself because customers are pushing
Arm used to sell only IP licenses with a 98.5% gross margin, never touching inventory or wafers. The step forward to compute subsystems already had customers grabbing pre-integrated 'subsystems' of CPU, GPU, and memory as modules. Going further, because 'customers wanting general-purpose CPUs for the large-model era couldn't find suppliers,' they came directly to Arm to place orders. Before the announcement, Arm asked nearly all licensees; opposition was minimal: a bigger software ecosystem benefits every customer, so Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google—companies making Arm server chips—all publicly supported it.

8:07 Banning AI tools is like sending engineers back to the library
The total chip design cycle is 24-36 months; the most time-consuming part is not RTL generation or architecture mapping but verification, validation, debugging, and documentation. AI is especially suited to these tasks. Internally, about 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily; turning off the tools would be like in the 1990s letting people use the internet only two hours a day and sending them back to the library downstairs for the rest. Currently AI's weakest areas are RTL generation and physical design, because models rely on public corpora while the industry's most critical details are private data—exactly the gap companies like Arm can fill.

10:35 From idea to tapeout takes five years, not two or three
When asked whether AI, by eating the most time-consuming verification step, could shrink the 24-36 months to 6-12, Rene Haas gave a measured answer: 2-3 years is unrealistic; beyond five years, for designs with less complex constraints, going from idea all the way to GDSII (the tapeout file handed to the foundry) is possible. If you feed the tool 'make a chip 10% faster, 20% cheaper, 30% more power-efficient than a reference,' don't expect a one-click result. His judgment: in 5-10 years, the industry's design methodology will change markedly.

15:00 AI supply and demand are far apart; the bottleneck is construction sites, not wafers
Discussing the AI bubble, Rene Haas distinguished between stock-level valuation froth and the industry chain itself; he stated clearly that supply 'is still far from' demand. Transformer inference and training consume both compute and memory, so demand won't stop. The real hard constraint will shift to data center construction: many projects are being delayed and need more manpower, and there is growing resistance to new data centers in various places. Over the next 3-5 years, the constraint may not be wafer capacity or memory but the persistently tight physical construction.

17:14 SoftBank's cloud move gives chip companies a customer
For chip/AI entrepreneurs with heavy assets and strong capex: capital availability itself is a gate, and strategic partnerships should reach the supply chain, PE, and bank levels early. Behind Arm is SoftBank, not just as a shareholder; SoftBank just announced plans for a 'neo cloud'-type service, allowing young chip companies to avoid only knocking on Microsoft's or Google's door for design wins, instead forming direct customer relationships with the Arm/SoftBank ecosystem—an extra path to adoption.

21:25 Humanoids won't unify; specialized robots will coexist long-term
Rene Haas believes robot 1.0 is purpose-built: mechanics and software are optimized for a single action, and changing a production line almost means starting over. New-generation robots that can redefine tasks through training and have a general-purpose mechanical body will first eat repetitive labor in construction, infrastructure, and security. Form factors won't converge on a single direction: factories, warehouses, and tools are all designed to human dimensions, giving humanoids an advantage; other tasks are better suited to specialized forms. Costs must come down first, and delivery and warehousing will be the earliest automated scenarios.

27:13 Chip restrictions on China are an unwinnable infinite game
On U.S. manufacturing, he is direct: America should build more fabs domestically, for both national security and supply chain diversification. On export controls, he speaks of an 'infinite game'—restricting chips to China cannot produce a victory with an end; it may instead drive key technologies out of the U.S. He also denies that data centers are 'big warehouses without jobs': the ecosystem around energy, liquid cooling, and more can create jobs in America.

36:00 In the token world, every path goes through the CPU
Using the token factory metaphor for accelerators, Rene Haas thinks the real system question is: who orchestrates and arbitrates where tokens go and delivers them to users? He believes every path goes through the CPU: beyond training, there is inference scheduling, system orchestration, context and tool invocation. At the edge, on devices that can't fit a 50W GPU, Arm's power advantage is more pronounced. The CPU hasn't disappeared; instead, it creates sustained demand alongside accelerators.

item.title: The Top Warning Sign of Financial Fraud: Not Greed, but Personal Financial Trouble
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/
item.description: For 14 consecutive years, the ACFE has ranked "personal financial problems" as the number one warning sign of financial misconduct; systemic incentives, the shutdown of critical brain regions, and moral overconfidence can all push good people across the line step by step.
item.content:encoded:
For 14 consecutive years, the ACFE has ranked "personal financial problems" as the number one warning sign of financial misconduct; systemic incentives, the shutdown of critical brain regions, and moral overconfidence can all push good people across the line step by step.

The two authors are a clinical neuropsychologist and a lawyer with 20 years of experience prosecuting financial advisors; their profile of wrongdoers and warning signs offer more diagnostic value than moral slogans.

2:04 The test for crossing the line is: this is not your money
Moira defines financial misconduct as "doing bad things with other people's money": both taking money for oneself and guiding or advising others to use funds in ways that are not in their best interest. She stresses that anyone working in finance should always remember "this is not your money." Reducing the ethical problem to fiduciary duty gives a unified benchmark for the warning signs that follow.

9:10 For 14 straight years, the top warning sign is personal financial trouble
Philippa cites the ACFE's global report: for 14 consecutive years, the number one warning sign of fraud has not been greed but "personal financial problems"—people whose personal finances are out of control, who cannot make ends meet, or who are deeply in debt are the most likely to become involved in financial misconduct. The financial industry offers access to other people's money and attracts people who seek wealth, and when you add people's irrationality around money, these three conditions combine into fertile ground for misconduct.

13:14 When taking advice, the brain is like praying: critical regions go offline
Moira notes that neuroimaging evidence shows that when people receive financial advice, key critical regions of the brain "go offline," a state similar to the brain during prayer. People feel safe, trusting, and open; this non-critical state increases vulnerability, especially for those unfamiliar with finance. She gives the example that even hedge fund managers will "sit and wait for the answer" in front of an advisor, without asking how the product actually works.

19:19 Good people go wrong starting with obedience and helpfulness, not greed
Philippa and Moira break down the path of good people going wrong: blindly obeying orders, crossing lines out of "misguided helpfulness," then hiding mistakes out of fear, and covering with bigger lies. The book's "John" slides from a small mistake to lying, then to doubling down on concealment. Moira emphasizes that ethics is not a solo sport but a team sport; if organizational culture tacitly permits misconduct, individuals find it hard to stay clean.

37:36 Psychopaths disproportionately flow into finance
Responding to Cameron's concern, Moira says the evidence shows that psychopaths disproportionately enter finance and business because "that's where the money is." She cites Robert Hare's research: successful psychopaths are often charming and extremely skilled at detecting and exploiting others' desires. The damage they cause is large, and they often continue moving within the industry because colleagues feel "relief" when they leave, passing the problem to the next firm.

53:50 Most people never realize they are making an ethical decision
Traditional ethics training always presents clear ethical dilemmas in the classroom, but real-world problems often emerge quietly, so people do not realize they are at a fork in the road. Moira cites Kahneman's "what you see is all there is": people do not proactively question the motives of product providers, do not think about who benefits from complex products, and do not admit they actually do not understand. The result is that even with ethics training, most of the time people do not even know they are facing an ethical decision.

1:02:56 The future wrongdoer is a vulnerable ordinary person, not a villain
Philippa lists the profile of the future wrongdoer: early in their career (Evan was involved in global fraud within a month of joining and was permanently banned after nine months), in debt, highly dependent on their boss, a people-pleaser, with low self-esteem (compensating with luxury cars), fatigued, and having family problems. These signals are rarely used by the industry to screen advisors' own biases; they are not rare evil but common weaknesses of ordinary people under stress and vulnerability.

1:09:07 After 20 years of prosecutions, never once sued a CFP holder
Philippa has been a lawyer for 20 years and has prosecuted many financial practitioners, but she has never sued any CFP designee. She believes there is no simple way to pick a good advisor, but obtaining certification is a positive signal. She also offers a criterion: if an advisor only talks about investments and does not understand the client's whole life situation, that is wealth management, not financial planning—planning is about the person, not the assets.

item.title: US Bond Yields Above 5% Aren't About Inflation: $32 Trillion in Debt Means Buyers Only Accept Higher Prices
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.description: Inflation can't explain the 30-year breaking 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, buyers already allocated at 5.3% won't bite for another $10 billion. What's really lifting the curve is the roughly $2 trillion in annual Treasury supply, which the Treasury can't suppress with buybacks.
item.content:encoded:
Inflation can't explain the 30-year breaking 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, buyers already allocated at 5.3% won't bite for another $10 billion. What's really lifting the curve is the roughly $2 trillion in annual Treasury supply, which the Treasury can't suppress with buybacks.

The mainstream narrative blames inflation for the 30-year at 5%; this episode offers a genuinely incremental alternative framework, folding the Treasury's intervention limits, the Fed's balance-sheet mechanics, and the term-premium debate into one coherent logic.

4:04 5% Is First the Treasury's Interest Bill, Not a Macro Signal
Host Joe asks Daryl what he sees when the 30-year Treasury yield is above 5%—even after a modest pullback following the Fed chair's speech that day. Daryl's answer isn't a macro model but the Treasury's predicament: if I were Treasury secretary, I'd see extremely high interest costs for the US government and would have to find ways to push yields down. That line sets the episode's frame: the official side has a strong incentive to suppress long-end rates, but whether it can and should is the premise for all that follows.

5:07 To Sell Another $10 Billion, the Treasury Must Pay Higher Interest
Daryl offers the episode's core thought experiment: suppose there's no inflation risk and no sovereign default, and you're a macro hedge fund already holding $20 billion in 10-year Treasuries. The Treasury secretary calls and asks you to buy another $10 billion—why would you refuse? The answer: you've already made your desired allocation at a 5.3% yield; to get you to add more, they must pay a higher rate to compensate. This logic also illustrates the structural shift on the demand side—foreign central banks have already bought enough and are no longer adding, so new Treasury supply must land on domestic free discretionary buyers: banks, pensions, insurers, hedge funds—money that is highly yield-sensitive.

8:10 It's Not That the Logic Changed; Debt Has Hit a Tipping Point
Joe raises the objection that must be faced: the bearish logic of aging populations, a political system unwilling to cut spending, and unsustainable deficits existed in 2018 and 2019, and Japan was told the same story for decades—so why did yields fall then and rise now? Daryl's answer is scale: the IMF's old 60% debt-to-GDP red line is far in the rearview mirror, with France already at 100%; the US Treasury market has grown from about $18 trillion to $31 trillion and keeps expanding. There's no new logic; the sheer quantity of debt has accumulated to a tipping point.

10:13 The Long End at 5% Is Driven by Supply, Not Inflation Expectations
Since the short end is still constrained by high inflation and the Fed, why can't the 30-year's high yield be directly attributed to inflation expectations? Daryl concedes that inflation over the past five years has been significantly above the Fed's target and that hitting the target is still incomplete, but he notes that implied inflation expectations derived from real and nominal bonds aren't flashing alarm; investors actually trading 10-, 20-, and 30-year Treasuries are processing supply relative to demand first, not inflation. He mentions John Cochrane's fiscal theory of the price level, but that's a long-run framework—the current driver of term premia is issuance volume, not prices.

13:18 Buybacks to Cap Yields Are a Signal, Not Enough Ammunition
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an expansion of Treasury buybacks, with the official rationale being liquidity. Daryl reads between the lines directly: from the wording of his public remarks, he doesn't think the problem is market liquidity; he thinks yields are 'too high,' and he explicitly says he's sending a signal to the market. The problem is that the scale of Treasury operations is a drop in the bucket relative to the entire Treasury market; the market moved briefly on the news and then quickly reversed. Trying to use government resources to suppress yield trends has precedent in the 1992 pound sterling attack—and Bessent was then the person shorting sterling at Soros's fund.

19:22 Buybacks' Real Job Is Cleaning Up Old Bonds, Not Managing Rates
The original design of the buyback program wasn't to manage yields: as the Treasury keeps issuing new bonds, the market accumulates a large stock of off-the-run issues that have lost liquidity, clogging dealer balance sheets and trading at prices that deviate from a smooth yield curve. Daryl's paper with two New York Fed economists tests whether buying back odd lots on a 'regular, predictable' schedule and reissuing new bonds can improve market liquidity and earn a buy-low-sell-high profit for taxpayers. The term 'odd lots' is, of course, the show's namesake. He thinks this routine operation is effective; the Treasury stepping in to defend its own bond market in an emergency is another matter.

25:30 The Constraint on Shrinking the Balance Sheet Is Reserves, Not Assets
The new Fed chair wants to shrink the balance sheet, but most people only watch the asset side. Daryl points out the arithmetic constraint: selling assets must be matched by an equal reduction in liabilities. Of the three liability components, the TGA can't have the Treasury withdraw its deposits, and currency in circulation can't be recalled; the only compressible piece is bank reserves held at the Fed. But today's reserves are the 'Swiss Army knife' of the financial industry: they earn interest at market rates, satisfy liquidity regulation, and are available for payments at any time—banks have no incentive to give them up. The ratchet effect Acharya and Rajan identified at Jackson Hole in 2017 already showed that every time the Fed expands, banks become addicted to reserves, and shrinking inevitably causes market volatility.

28:33 The Task Force Will Swap Duration, Not Truly Shrink
Daryl says he has no inside information on the task force, but he makes two predictions about the group led by Jeremy Stein: first, the real problem is structure, not size; the sensible approach is to gradually replace the Fed's long-term Treasury holdings with short-term bills, so that interest expense on the liability side (reserves) moves in the same direction as interest income on the asset side (bills), reducing the impact of policy-rate volatility on the Fed's own P&L. Second, don't keep mortgage-backed securities on the asset side; let them run off naturally. His own conclusion is blunter: the Fed may not actually need to shrink, but it must have tools it can use to shrink on its own, or it will be backed into a corner when Congress pressures it.

item.title: The Profit Secret of Wallets Isn't Balance Interest, It's Money Circulating Within the System
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.description: The core accounting of a wallet: money coming in incurs card network fees, internal transfers are nearly free, and withdrawals can be charged again; it earns from the spread of movement, not from idle balance interest. PayPal, Cash App, and Stripe Link are all betting on this model.
item.content:encoded:
The core accounting of a wallet: money coming in incurs card network fees, internal transfers are nearly free, and withdrawals can be charged again; it earns from the spread of movement, not from idle balance interest. PayPal, Cash App, and Stripe Link are all betting on this model.

This episode breaks down the real cost structure of wallets: wholesale channel fees are less than a cent, yet platforms can charge users several cents; Japanese peers even open multiple bank accounts to bypass clearing. Even if you're not in payments, this serves as a business teardown template.

1:05 A wallet must answer how it makes money from day one
The episode opens with a $100 Venmo payment to a barber, questioning why PayPal still wants to insert itself into such small transactions that already have mature payment rails. It then quickly defines the scope: this is about e-wallet businesses, not crypto private-key wallets. A wallet that appears to hold balances immediately enters the regulatory sensitive zone of deposits, so from day one it must answer how it makes money—if it can't, the product dies.

5:14 Card fraud isn't from fake merchant sites, it's from issuer-side leaks
The biggest early obstacle to online transactions was users' reluctance to hand over card numbers, with media repeatedly hyping the risk of card theft. The author points out the opposite is true: much fraud comes from massive data leaks on the issuing side, not from scammers building fake sites, concluding that 'economies of scale also protect criminals.' PayPal's value is shielding users between their card number and the payee, limiting the risk of each transaction—this justifies charging close to 3% in network fees and plants the seed for the later balance design.

6:19 A free wallet is anything but free for the wallet itself
Putting money into a wallet requires going through card networks, historically about 3%, a cost borne by the wallet. But once balances stay within the system, transfers between users are almost like editing a database row—so cheap they can't be billed. PayPal charges near the original price for both inbound and outbound, so simply substituting internal transfers for external ones yields extra gross margin. A wallet that seems free to users is not free for the wallet—the zero marginal cost of existing balances is the real moat.

9:21 Driving down network fees beats product innovation for profits
There's no inherent link between wholesale and retail: buying millions of ACH transactions costs about $0.05 each, yet payment service providers can charge merchants nearly $0.30; the difference is the tax platforms levy on the underlying rails. Japan is more extreme: interbank transfers cost about ¥200 per transaction, while intra-bank entries are nearly free, so some products open accounts at major banks, move users' money internally, and settle via daily netting. In the financial world, reducing network fees translates more directly into wallet profits than product innovation.

12:27 Withdrawals aren't a user perk; they're a second revenue pipeline
Cash App prices withdrawals too: for speed, you choose the more expensive card rail, at 1.75% with a $0.25 minimum; the author tested withdrawing $50 and was quoted $0.88. Complementing this is partnering with institutions like Sutton Bank to issue prepaid cards, so spending outside the system also earns interchange. Wallets no longer treat withdrawals as a user benefit but as a second income stream, because partner banks need the wallet's user base, and the wallet needs the bank's issuing license.

20:53 Co-branded cards earn a cut but carry the credit risk
The logic of wallet-issued credit cards is two-way charging, but risk control is the real battleground: wallets typically assume their accumulated spending data can underwrite better than the issuing bank. The industry has repeatedly shown that FICO is already so strong it's hard to beat; additional variables that materially improve losses often cross legal red lines. What truly prices the wallet is the agreement—banks require the entire loan portfolio's loss rate to stay below a threshold, or the wallet's revenue share drops to zero or even goes negative. 10-K language avoids 'loss sharing,' but in essence the wallet is absorbing the issuer's bad debts.

24:50 Users care about the phone, not the card
Apple's core argument to banks is that users care about their phones, not the plastic credit card; if banks don't pay up, Apple could support or build a new two-sided payment network and take users with it. Reports say Apple takes 15 basis points per Apple Pay transaction, while Google reportedly takes nothing—the author uses this to mock the two giants' differing abilities in non-core products. The deeper layer is that the checkout itself can be like an ad slot: when product and price are set, who gets placed first in the payment options becomes an auction. Stripe has already shifted from static display to dynamic sorting based on user preferences, even allowing merchants to fine-tune options.

31:13 Network fees aren't lowered at the negotiating table but in default settings
Extend Link as a ledger-level settlement negotiation layer: if users store their low-fee payment methods in Link, the next checkout can bypass card networks and go through bank accounts; the saved network fees are then redistributed between merchants and users. This solution can't be achieved by one company sitting at a table; it's the aggregation of millions of users' and merchants' decisions, ultimately giving the party on the other side of the payment negotiation table a scale close to 1% of global GDP. Only that scale can force network fees to be repriced.

item.title: No Quantum Gravity, No Real AGI
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.description: A physicist draws a high bar for AGI: it must solve quantum gravity. This conversation also clarifies the real relationship between quantum materials and AI—once the synthesizability filter is applied, the discovered materials may number zero.
item.content:encoded:
A physicist draws a high bar for AGI: it must solve quantum gravity. This conversation also clarifies the real relationship between quantum materials and AI—once the synthesizability filter is applied, the discovered materials may number zero.

A noise-canceling listen for the AI world's default assumptions: a string theorist makes scientific payoffs and AI boundaries concrete and testable, useful for calibrating your own timelines in hard tech. The pace is slow; the core arguments cluster in the middle and later sections.

17:28 Too much learning paralyzes; naivety is needed to ask original questions
The hardest step from student to researcher is not absorbing knowledge but posing original questions that push the boundary of knowledge. Gopakumar describes this leap as 'naivety plus experience': learning too much can paralyze you, and you need to retain a bit of naivety to dare ask questions that seem intractable. A mentor's role is to teach you to break big questions into small steps you can advance today without losing the ultimate goal. His mentor David Gross excelled at this—according to Gopakumar, Gross's first student produced work that won a Nobel Prize for both, and Witten also received a Fields Medal. Now he trains his own students with the same method: he assigns the first one or two problems, for which he himself has no answer, and accompanies them through to their third or fourth year before letting them pose questions independently.

28:36 Spacetime is not a backdrop but an emergent approximation
Using 'water composed of discrete atoms' as an analogy for string theory: the continuous spacetime we touch is likely a low-resolution approximation of a deeper structure at macroscopic scales. Gopakumar stresses this is not pure speculation—quantum mechanics itself does not allow treating spacetime as an infinitely divisible smooth backdrop; plus black holes (which Hawking and others found to have many anomalous properties) and the failure at the Big Bang singularity force physicists to ask where spacetime comes from. String theory offers a natural framework: spacetime emerges from something more fundamental, and gravity along with the known interactions can be accommodated. This explains why he sets 'solving quantum gravity' as a high bar for intelligence: it demands not just problem-solving but the creation of new conceptual frameworks.

39:45 Materials should be designed in reverse: specify properties first, then find structure
He first gives a long-term scale: quantum mechanics was initially only for understanding atoms, but now the devices it underpins account for an estimated 35%-40% of US GDP, and commercial ripples only became visible four to five decades after the theory emerged. He calls the current phase the second quantum revolution: quantum materials like graphene, discovered by accident, are already being commercialized. The next step is AI-driven inverse materials design—first define the desired properties, then search for structures that achieve them and how to synthesize them, bypassing traditional trial-and-error chemistry. He also reveals a conversation with Demis Hassabis: DeepMind's next holy grail is finding a room-temperature superconductor, and Hassabis warned him at the outset not to talk about quantum gravity.

50:59 Getting stuck is the norm; keep three or four problems in play at once
Being stuck is not the exception but the daily reality of a researcher; especially during the transition from student to researcher, being stuck can feel crushing. Gopakumar's first strategy is portfolio hedging: work on three or four problems simultaneously, and if one dies, switch to another; probabilistically, at least one will move forward a half-step. His second tactic is to teach—when students' eyes light up, that satisfaction can pull you out of a low, and he has often found that 'after a lecture, a stuck problem suddenly opens up.' His third is to deliberately learn something new you have always wanted to study but never had time for, gaining a fresh frame of reference before returning to the old problem.

55:08 Talent is multiplicative, not additive; headcount is never the missing ingredient
Why does top-tier science concentrate in a few places rather than spread uniformly? Gopakumar offers a mechanism: being in the same place, conversing, and using each other as sounding boards keeps the brain stimulated even without formal collaboration; when collaboration does happen, the different skills of two people multiply rather than add. He borrows a physics metaphor: photons in an ordinary light bulb are chaotic, while those in a laser are coherent; once a group achieves coherence, it can produce a lasing effect. He says many Indian institutions underperform relative to their talent—what is missing is not headcount but this resonant atmosphere. Hence ICTS's founding principle is simple: hire only first-rate people, give them resources and freedom, and do not let them lower their ambitions.

1:11:19 AI can accelerate research but cannot make conceptual leaps
AI just won two Nobel Prizes in quick succession, but Gopakumar splits 'AI for science' from 'science for AI': the former he acknowledges as an overdrive gear—AI is accelerating a narrow class of tasks in research. Yet the 'theory' AI does today is far from his conceptual standard; the best physics relies on conceptual leaps, not pattern recognition. Conversely, he is more optimistic about science for AI—among those who discovered scaling laws at Anthropic, some have physics backgrounds; Hopfield himself is a statistical physicist who used simple physical models to simulate the brain. Along this path, physicists may join computer scientists and neuroscientists to move AI from language models to physics-inspired world models. This distinction is worth remembering.

1:21:32 After the synthesizability filter, AI-discovered materials number zero
The most sobering cold water in the whole talk comes from the Q&A: Google claims AI has discovered a large number of new materials, but after filtering for feasibility and synthesizability, Gopakumar says, 'I think left with zero.' His stance is not to dismiss AI materials science (someone in the audience cites Microsoft's use of a DFT model with only 385,000 parameters, bypassing traditional hybrid methods), but to remind that the chain is long: after predicting crystal structures, you still need to grow them and scale them up, and each step can filter out surprises. He says India should also bet on this chain. This statement is a useful counter-calibration for the 'AI discovers new materials' narrative.

item.title: AI Leaders Are Refineries, Not Winners of Native Apps
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.description: AI enters the agent era: first-phase leaders are just refineries, not winners of native apps; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations shift from roles to tasks; ultimately, humans compete on creativity that creates something from nothing.
item.content:encoded:
AI enters the agent era: first-phase leaders are just refineries, not winners of native apps; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations shift from roles to tasks; ultimately, humans compete on creativity that creates something from nothing.

Zeng Ming offers a three-phase industrial history framework to give you a coordinate system for locating AI's current position. It cures the optimism of "this time is different," and also provides realistic expectations for application entrepreneurs' opportunity windows and giants' transformation pains.

16:28 Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of general-purpose technologies into three stages: first becoming social infrastructure, then an explosion of applications, and finally the emergence of native applications. In 2026, the consensus on token as a unit of measurement signals the maturity of the first stage; the agent events around the Spring Festival (commonly called "lobster") mark AI's official entry into the agent era. He compares it to the website-building movement of 1992: back then people built websites to share information; today they build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet; whoever can establish agent standards and capture user entry points may be the biggest opportunity in the next two years.

27:49 A ten-trillion-dollar company will emerge, but not these two
Zeng Ming bluntly states that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technical and commercial achievements, but business history shows that the first wave of companies to run out are likely not the big winners of the native application stage. Yahoo was worth $120 billion five years after founding, and AOL reached a valuation of $220 billion, yet neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies, refineries that extract base oil; the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies—and cars were not made by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will definitely appear in the future, but it may not be the current leaders. Model companies will move toward a mature business of oligopoly plus strong government regulation.

1:10:29 The unit of AI-native organizations is tasks, not roles
Companies correspond to the hierarchical system of the industrial age. AI disrupts the industrial age, and the corporate system will decline. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not a role but a task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow according to "what problem needs solving," and both humans and AI collaborate around tasks. Therefore, well-designed positions and hierarchies will disappear, and traditional middle management will also die out. Future founders must first define the organizational task network. Silicon Valley's NewLab is a prototype of the new organizational form; OpenAI itself is more like a Lab than a traditional company. The culture of new organizations resembles a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing, and co-creation, not command and assessment.

1:31:32 Excellence is judged only in hindsight; being good is visible on the spot
Zeng Ming believes "excellent ≠ extraordinary." Excellence is growth sustained by positive feedback, while extraordinariness requires overcoming repeated negative feedback, persisting when everyone disapproves, and ultimately proving oneself a prophet of the era through enormous success. So "extraordinariness is determined after the fact." Those who are merely excellent easily fall into a cycle of self-validation, leading to conservative strategies. Extraordinary people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the era and partners, and are mission-driven rather than externally valuation-driven. When identifying founders, he asks, "What kind of self would you be satisfied with ten years from now?" If the answer is "a ten-billion-dollar company," that is mainly self-driven, not an inner mission. Truly extraordinary founders are often altruistic and empathetic.

1:47:24 Strategy in the AI era cannot be planned; it must be generated
In the AI era, strategy is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a "strategy generation system": organizations must establish an environment and network that allows strategic insights to emerge naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality requirements are higher, CEOs cannot rely on linear extrapolation for planning, nor can they outsource strategy to McKinsey—McKinsey's rise was a product of the slow maturity of the industrial era. His methodology is "look ten years, think three years, act one year," with the core being "think three years": you must see at least two or three milestones ahead, creating tension between short-term actions and the medium-term picture. Organizational construction must ensure sufficient context rather than control, enabling the right people to make the right decisions at the right time.

2:01:39 The right analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
Zeng Ming believes robots are still in the strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. Currently there are two routes—building a generalized brain first or closing the loop in specific scenarios first—both logically valid, and it's impossible to judge in advance which is faster. Historically, the automobile industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and it wasn't until Ford built the assembly line in 1913 that it entered scale; robots haven't yet had their Model T moment, and whoever truly sells ten thousand robots first is already remarkable. But a better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented, refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, and countless other categories emerged. Robots interacting with the physical world will have N major scenarios, and home, companionship, and industrial uses may each produce their own native giants.

2:03:39 Giants that feel safe are the most unsafe
Zeng Ming says that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe; feeling safe is the most unsafe. In business history, no company has ever smoothly transitioned from one era to the next. IBM and Microsoft are the only two possible exceptions, and both are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that disrupts the industrial revolution, not a continuation innovation like mobile internet, so the technological reserves and organizational culture of old giants are liabilities. Google can survive as an AI cloud company, but it may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is not naturally safe either. New platforms are likely to be created by new companies.

2:20:56 Human value lies in creating from nothing, not in writing songs or painting
Borrowing Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the era of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI. Humans are both forced and finally liberated to develop new potential. This potential is creativity—not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and create something from nothing. AI has already taken all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. Therefore, he calls his mission "being a happy researcher" and believes the next step of civilization will reorganize around creativity. Even the education system will be forced to shift from "knowledge indoctrination" to "open exploration," because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

item.title: The Moat in AI Writing Isn't the Model—It's the Proprietary Data You Feed It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
item.description: Over two years, writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during unemployment into a one-person content engine and a compounding editor. The core method isn't prompt tricks—it's using proprietary experience to fill the 'last mile' the model can't reach.
item.content:encoded:
Over two years, writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during unemployment into a one-person content engine and a compounding editor. The core method isn't prompt tricks—it's using proprietary experience to fill the 'last mile' the model can't reach.

Not a tool review, but how a non-technical writer turned AI into a mode of production. The meat is in the last 30 minutes; the earlier personal story provides the motivational backdrop.

2:09 The biggest value of an AI coach isn't saving money
After being laid off, she was in a low point and couldn't afford a human career coach's hourly rate, but a $20-a-month ChatGPT subscription was acceptable. She found that writing out her thoughts and having AI question and push back from the outside helped her externalize thinking, counter catastrophizing, and gave her a sense of accountability. The most important legacy of this experience wasn't the money saved—it was the belief that AI could actually drive concrete change in her life. At the time, she was hesitating about whether to take Every's freelance offer; ChatGPT gave her a nudge to just try it.

8:26 Output comes from upfront context, not clever prompts
She once took on a delivery load of 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts, and 16 Instagram posts in a week and a half. She could do it not because she wrote smarter one-line prompts, but because she did a lot of upfront context engineering: feeding the model brand information, product details, audience profiles, and differentiators all at once. Much of the demand was essentially content reuse, and AI is good at rewriting a long article into versions for different platforms. Her rule: set up the scene early, and you can run fast later.

11:28 Give the model a fence before you talk tone and word choice
Before Claude Projects existed, she had to keep persistent documents in Google Docs and manually copy-paste them into the context each time. This structure didn't come out of nowhere—it's the style guide tradition in content marketing: first define who the audience is, what their pain points are, how the product addresses them, and where competitors and differentiators lie. She says this gives the model a fenced playground, ensuring it won't go off track before you even talk about word choice, tone, and reading level. When Projects launched, she set up a separate project for each client and each column.

15:40 The last mile of AI writing can only be filled by humans
She believes there's a 'last mile' problem in AI writing: models have a knowledge cutoff and don't live in the physical world. So the human's job is to supply the latest data and real experience that AI can't reach. She warns that if you just throw 'write a blog post about style guides' at the model, you'll get generic content it already knows—commodity information. What makes writing unique is the fresh ingredients the model hasn't seen: internal company research, third-party reports, personal experience. The writing system is the kitchen; the human provides the good ingredients.

22:50 AI's value is reducing friction, not speeding up output
She speaks openly about her bipolar disorder and points out that AI's value isn't just producing content faster—it's reducing friction in life. She put off booking a primary care physician for three years, then had Codex find a doctor who accepted her insurance and was taking new patients, and complete the appointment. Emails are first filtered by automation, and only those that truly need a human reply reach her inbox. She says this completely solved her email anxiety. This isn't using AI as a production tool, but as assistive technology that makes her daily operation 'as a person' easier.

27:03 Let AI interview you repeatedly, and it can prioritize for you
Two years ago she simply asked ChatGPT 'can you be my career coach.' Today that coach lives in a Codex project: it contains her job profile, Every's brand positioning, content performance data, a folder of reader praise, and OKRs. She doesn't maintain a dashboard herself; she uses voice conversations to have the system prioritize by highest impact, and the system maintains the Kanban for her. The key to building this system was letting AI interview her repeatedly, then distilling those conversations into context. She says it's like having a chief of staff, not just a writer.

32:27 Feedback that only fixes the current draft is wasted
The core of the Compound Writing plugin is a compounding mindset: every piece of feedback you give AI should flow back into the system so the next output is automatically better. She forked Kieran Klassen's Compound Engineering plugin and adapted it to a writing workflow: code and writing both have stages like brainstorming, planning, drafting, and review, except writing focuses more on structure, voice, and evidence. Editing is further split into a substantive edit that looks at big structure and argument, a line edit that handles sentence by sentence, and a final pass for pre-publication checks. Now she doesn't write in a web chat window; she feeds the day's fresh material into this system.

39:19 Vonnegut as editor gives perspective, not verdicts
She built Vonnegut's eight narrative elements, Hitchcock's suspense principle about the bomb under the table, and Sorkin's and Sedaris's ways of expression into the plugin as editing skills. Vonnegut checks 'does the story start as close to the end as possible' and 'does every sentence earn its place.' Hitchcock's lens asks whether the reader will want to keep reading. She stresses this isn't about having the masters' souls grade your draft—it's giving you a new perspective you can accept or reject. Non-professional writers might benefit even more because they're less likely to nitpick themselves while writing.

item.title: Stronger Models Make Dirty Data More Lethal: Cleaning Is Worth More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
item.description: Jane Street's alt data team finds that once data leaks future information into the past, stronger models become more dangerous; nailing down 'what was known at the time' is worth more than tuning the model.
item.content:encoded:
Jane Street's alt data team finds that once data leaks future information into the past, stronger models become more dangerous; nailing down 'what was known at the time' is worth more than tuning the model.

This episode is dense with how data engineering actually creates value; the latter half on corrections, timestamps, and cost models offers judgments you won't hear in most AI discussions.

2:06 Patterns get competed away once discovered
Eric defines this as an anti-inductive environment: in trading, patterns you find are often quickly digested by others and the market, then stop working; there is little knowledge that accumulates like physical laws. Because of this, the signal-to-noise ratio in trading data is naturally poor—the whole market mechanism constantly squeezes out extractable signals, leaving what approaches a random walk. To keep winning, you must keep finding new facts, not cling to old patterns.

19:21 Prices can go negative; don't hardcode assumptions
On April 20, 2020, CME crude futures near expiry settled at a negative price—just that one day, and the final settlement later turned positive. The reason wasn't that oil had no value, but that storage at Cushing, the delivery point, was nearly full and no one wanted to take physical delivery. Order entry and risk systems that long assumed prices must be positive failed on the spot: some couldn't place orders, others didn't know how to handle negative returns. Eric's conclusion: a large part of trading is understanding the messy details of reality—storage capacity, contract multipliers, quote units—and getting those details right in systems is what caps risk.

32:33 Domain experts don't know how good tools can be
For data and systems to be truly usable, the bottleneck is often not writing code but translation. Eric observes that traders have high tolerance for clunky processes, worn down by Excel and manual workflows to the point they don't know they deserve better tools; conversely, software engineers who don't understand the trading domain can only build to a narrow spec. So his job is to explain the real mechanics of the domain to engineers and 'how good it could be' to traders. At Jane Street, every desk now has such an embedded developer, a role that grew out of this need.

59:04 Parking spots don't equal sales
A classic alt data example is counting cars in Walmart parking lots, assuming more people means better business. Eric says this example is actually poor: what you want to infer is spend, and spots only tell you foot traffic, quite indirect; about 20% of Walmart purchases happen online, and cities like New York have no lots to count. More direct signals sit on the transaction side: issuing banks, Visa/Mastercard networks, and credit union processing systems know what people actually spend, and can sell anonymized aggregates to buy-side firms.

1:04:08 Corrected data turns backtests into time machines
When deciding whether to subscribe to a dataset, the vendor may have already corrected past errors; backtesting on that clean data tests not what you would have received in real time, but the correct answers known only later. Eric says that's like simulating having a time machine. Jane Street's solution: save every raw file and the local timestamp of receipt, so no matter how many transformations you do later, you can reconstruct 'what we knew at that moment.' This mirrors the logic of distrusting exchange timestamps and trusting only your own data arrival time.

1:08:10 LLMs know the future; keep them away from historical data
AI hits alt data in two ways: stronger predictive models raise the value of good data, and LLMs make feature extraction from text easier. But there's a causal trap—using the latest LLM to featurize old documents brings in later knowledge: it knows Enron's eventual fate, and may have seen subsequent revisions of a financial report in its training data. That creates new future leakage, especially when processing historical data; you must pin down 'which model version at which point in time.'

1:11:26 Stronger models make data cleaning more valuable
A common expectation is that as neural nets get stronger, feature engineering and manual cleaning will be replaced. Eric thinks the opposite: once models can do more themselves, you need less manual feature work, but the data fed in must be more correct. If data isn't point-in-time and leaks future information into the past, stronger models will learn that problem; different models also have varying tolerance for outliers and dirty patches. Net, cleaning data becomes more valuable, not less.

1:16:34 Usage-based pricing tempts teams to nickel-and-dime
Jane Street runs its data warehouse in-house, not purely out of control issues. Eric's observation: moving the same queries to a cloud vendor priced by read volume or compute time gets expensive enough that you think 'that money could buy a pile of hardware.' More importantly, the cost model distorts behavior—usage-based pricing makes teams constantly optimize bills and reshape workloads to fit billing; self-hosting turns cost into a one-time hardware investment, so teams spend time on research and queries, not saving money.

item.title: The Most Valuable Step in Writing with AI Isn't the Prompt—It's Turning Edit Feedback into Compound Interest
